newsitem.title: USA: FEATURE-Seaport Museum keeps alive NY's 19th century past.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Seaport Museum keeps alive NY's 19th century past.

text.p: One hundred and fifty years ago longshoremen thronged southern Manhattan's piers searching for work on the hundreds of schooners and barges that sailed daily into what was then the world's greatest port.

Today, though the pace at the tip of the island is as frenetic as ever, the landscape has changed. Gone are the 80-foot (24 metre) masted schooners and 400-foot (122 metre)-long barges that once lined the port so thickly it was called the Street of Ships.
In their place are the skyscrapers and brokerage houses of 20th century commerce. Wall Street is just a short walk away.
But in the chaos of quick change, one small group of red-brick buildings has managed to survive as a reminder to New Yorkers and visitors of Manhattan's 19th century past.

The South Street Seaport Museum, housed in a landmark 11-block section of New York's financial district, has been run by a dedicated group of sailors and maritime enthusiasts since it opened in 1967. It has survived times of fiscal crisis in the city and persevered through a long history of official neglect of New York's once-vibrant shoreline.

"The great sailing centres of the world were Sydney, Hong Kong, San Francisco and New York. Many people here forget we have such a great maritime history. It shaped this city," the white-bearded museum president, Peter Neill, said. "It was from here that Americans transferred information, goods, people and ideas to other Americans and abroad."
MARTIME TRADE -- FOUNDATION OF FINANCIAL N.Y.

Maritime trade was the foundation for the financial centre the city has become. The port of New York grew into prominence after the Erie Canal opened in 1825 and gave the East Coast access to the wealth of the Midwest and Great Lakes. The movement of goods led to the building of trading houses, banks, shipbuilders and chandleries.

By 1845, the port of New York was the departure point of Europeans and East Coast Americans heading to California aboard Clipper ships in search of gold, and the port of call for tropical fruits, spices and other goods from abroad.

Through exhibits, lectures and its own fleet of six historic ships -- the largest private collection in the United States -- the museum chronicles the seamen and merchants as well as the saloons and brothels that crowded this district.

One of the most memorable ways the museum brings 19th century New York to life are its sailing trips for the public aboard the Pioneer, built in 1885. The last iron-hulled American merchant sailing vessel of its kind, the coastal schooner takes passengers into New York Harbour, cutting close to such historic sites as the Brooklyn Bridge, the Statue of Liberty and the former immigrant station at Ellis Island.

"You get more of a feel for the history of the harbour on a sail boat. There would have been hundreds of boats like the Pioneer coming in and out of the port," Zachary Thomas, a Pioneer captain and longtime sailor, said.
'SOME OF THE GREATEST BRIDGES EVER BUILT'

"When you are out there in the harbour you can see some of the greatest bridges ever built, forts used during the War of 1812, Ellis Island, the Statue of Liberty. It is probably one of the more unique sails in the East Coast," Thomas said.

With its rope rigging and thick ropes for heaving up five large sails, the Pioneer straddles time like a ghost ship out of a Jules Verne novel. It sails around the glass-and-steel towers of Wall Street and rocks in the wake of an exploding number of dinner boats, water taxis and cruise lines.

All this is part of the slow revitalisation of New York's waterfront that is drawing travelers from the city's better known landmarks and inland tourist traps. Only recently the city began to focus on its hundreds of miles of shoreline and draft a plan to reclaim the piers that fell silent with the advent of container ships in the 1960s and the transfer of commerce to nearby New Jersey.
Already, plans are under way for ecology centres, bikeways around Manhattan island and sports playing fields.

Looking out at the harbour as the massive Pioneer sailed into dock, Neill reflected on what he describes as a new dynamic: "Until recently the city has been systematically destroying the waterfront. Now there is a refined and effective movement to bring people back to the water. In many ways, I think we started that."
